procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 13th February, 1981 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Writ Petitions Nos. 5458 and 5459 of 1980.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court granted 'leave' (presumably a certificate) to appeal to the Supreme Court on an oral application by the Advocate General. The High Court stated that the question of whether Section 129-A of the Motor Vehicles Act is ultra vires the Constitution, infringing Article 19(1)(g), relates to the interpretation of the Constitution and is a substantial question of law of general importance.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The case reached the Supreme Court via Civil Appeals No. 2546-2547 of 1983, after the High Court granted leave to appeal. Additionally, some operators directly approached the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution with writ petitions, which were heard along with the civil appeals.

directions: The appeals are allowed with costs and the writ petitions filed in High Court are dismissed.
Their writ petitions have been heard along with the civil appeals and for the same reasons they are dismissed with costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution requiring it to be heard by a bench of at least five judges under Article 145(3).

facts: The High Court granted a certificate to appeal to the Supreme Court.
The High Court's order stated that the question 'relates to the interpretation of the Constitution' and is also a 'substantial question of law of general importance'.
However, the High Court did not explicitly certify that the case involved a 'substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution'.
law: Article 145(3) of the Constitution requires a minimum of five judges to decide a case involving a 'substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution'.
A certificate for appeal based on a substantial question of constitutional interpretation is granted under Article 132.
A certificate for appeal based on a 'substantial question of law of general importance' is granted under Article 133.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the specific wording of the High Court's certificate.

It found that the High Court used the precise language of Article 133 ('a substantial question of law of general importance') and had 'refrained from certifying' it under the terms of Article 132 ('a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution').
Therefore, the Court treated the certificate as one granted under Article 133, not Article 132.
The Supreme Court also independently stated that it was 'satisfied that the cases do not involve a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the issue, concluding that a five-judge bench was not required under Article 145(3). This was because the High Court's certificate was granted under Article 133, not Article 132, and the Supreme Court itself determined that no substantial question of constitutional interpretation was involved.

issue.issue_text: Whether there is a lacuna in the law regarding the proper custody and disposal of a motor vehicle seized under Section 129-A of the Motor Vehicles Act, thereby affecting its validity.

law.name: Section 129-A of the Motor Vehicles Act
law.description: Authorizes a police officer or other authorized person to seize and temporarily detain a motor vehicle if they have reason to believe it is being used without a valid certificate of registration or permit.

law.name: Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.)
law.description: A procedural law that governs the administration of criminal law in India. The Court found its provisions on property custody and disposal to be applicable.

law.name: Section 451 of the Cr.P.C.
law.description: Empowers a court to make orders for the proper custody of any property produced before it during an inquiry or trial, pending the conclusion of the proceedings.

law.name: Section 452 & Chapter XXXIV of the Cr.P.C.
law.description: Grants the court power, at the conclusion of a case, to make appropriate orders for the disposal of property regarding which an offense appears to have been committed.

law.name: Section 91 of the Cr.P.C.
law.description: Gives the court the power to compel the production of any document or thing, including the seized vehicle.

application.description: The Court established that the Motor Vehicles Act does not operate in isolation. It must be read in conjunction with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
The Court noted that Section 129-A itself describes the detention as "temporary" and for "safe custody." This temporary period lasts until a court can make appropriate orders.

The Court explained that once a formal complaint is filed in court regarding the offense, the court acquires jurisdiction over the seized vehicle. The vehicle is considered to have been "produced" before the court at this point.

For custody of the vehicle *during* the trial, the Court pointed to Section 451 of the Cr.P.C. This section explicitly allows the court to make any order it deems fit for the proper custody of the property until the case is concluded.

For the final disposal of the vehicle *after* the trial, the Court relied on Section 452 and Chapter XXXIV of the Cr.P.C. These provisions empower the court to pass final orders on how to dispose of the vehicle, especially if it was used in the commission of an offense.

The Court also mentioned that if there were any doubt, Section 91 of the Cr.P.C. gives it ample power to compel the production of the vehicle, ensuring it can always exercise control over the seized property.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that there is a lacuna in the law. It held that when the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act are read together with the comprehensive procedures for property custody and disposal found in the Code of Criminal Procedure, there is a complete and sufficient legal framework to handle a vehicle seized under Section 129-A. Therefore, the section is valid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there is a lacuna in the law regarding the proper custody and disposal of a motor vehicle seized under Section 129-A of the Motor Vehicles Act, thereby affecting its validity.
appellant_arguments: The procedure for seizure under the Motor Vehicles Act is unreasonable because it does not comply with the provisions of Section 100 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which deals with searches and the preparation of a list of seized items.
respondent_arguments: There is no lacuna in the law, as Section 4(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure stipulates that offences under other laws (like the Motor Vehicles Act) are to be dealt with according to the Code's provisions.

Once a complaint is filed in court regarding the offence for which the vehicle was seized, the court acquires jurisdiction to pass appropriate orders regarding the custody and disposal of the vehicle.
Section 100 of the Criminal Procedure Code is not applicable because it deals with searches, not seizures of a vehicle under the Motor Vehicles Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Whenever an offence is committed under a law other than the Penal Code, and that special law does not itself regulate the complete procedure to be followed, the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be applied to investigate, inquire into, try, and otherwise deal with the offence, weaving the provisions of the code and the special law into a single texture.
obiter: A certificate for appeal granted by a High Court that employs the precise language of Article 133(1) of the Constitution is to be treated as a certificate under that article, even if it also mentions that the question relates to the interpretation of the Constitution without specifically certifying it as a substantial question of constitutional interpretation under Article 132.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that Section 129-A of the Motor Vehicles Act is constitutionally valid. The High Court erred by failing to consider the interplay between the Motor Vehicles Act and the Code of Criminal Procedure. When read together, these statutes provide a complete and reasonable scheme for the seizure, custody, and disposal of a vehicle involved in an offence, thus filling any perceived procedural lacunae and negating the claim that the provision is an unreasonable restriction on fundamental rights.
legal_tests_applied: Article 145(3) of the Constitution: The court assessed whether the case involved a 'substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution' to determine if a five-judge bench was mandatory.

Article 133 of the Constitution: The court analyzed the language of the High Court's certificate to determine that it was granted on the basis of a 'substantial question of law of general importance' under this article, not for constitutional interpretation.

Harmonious Construction of Statutes: The court reasoned that the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act must be examined in light of the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure to understand the complete legal framework governing the seizure of a vehicle in connection with an offence.
why_appellant_lost: The contention that there is a lacuna in the law was rejected because the court found that the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act and the Code of Criminal Procedure are interlaced, creating a comprehensive scheme for dealing with a seized vehicle.

The argument that the seizure lacked a discernible purpose was incorrect, as the court identified its purposes as preventing the repetition of the offence and preserving the vehicle as material evidence for prosecution.

The High Court's reasons for finding the law unconstitutional, such as the lack of provisions for confiscation, custody, or appeal within the Motor Vehicles Act itself, do not bear scrutiny when the Act is properly examined alongside the Code of Criminal Procedure.
why_respondent_won: The request for a five-judge bench was denied because the High Court's certificate was granted under Article 133 (substantial question of general importance), not for a substantial question of constitutional interpretation, and the Supreme Court itself was satisfied that no such constitutional question was involved.

The court accepted that the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to offences committed under other laws, like the Motor Vehicles Act, thereby providing the necessary procedures for handling property seized during the commission of an offence.
The court affirmed the validity of Section 129-A of the Motor Vehicles Act, finding that it did not infringe upon the fundamental right guaranteed by Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
policy_considerations: Whenever property involved in the commission of an offence is seized, the seizure is generally expected to serve a manifold purpose such as to prevent repetition of the offence, to use the thing seized as material evidence in the prosecution, and to preserve the property to enable the court to pass appropriate orders.
